explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - GoogleTest is not a full-stack app but an open-source C++ testing and mocking framework.  
   - It’s composed of two tightly coupled libraries:  
     • googletest (the xUnit-style C++ test runner)  
     • googlemock (the C++ mocking framework)  
   - The repo also contains documentation (Jekyll-based), build configurations (Bazel & CMake), CI scripts, and sample tests.

2. Analyze the file structure  
   - Top-level directories and files:  
     • BUILD.bazel, CMakeLists.txt, WORKSPACE – multi-platform build orchestrators  
     • ci/ – platform-specific presubmit scripts (Linux, macOS, Windows)  
     • docs/ – Jekyll site sources for GitHub Pages  
     • googlemock/ – headers, sources, tests, CMake integration for mocking  
     • googletest/ – headers, sources, tests, CMake integration for the core test framework  
   - Patterns: modular design (two libraries), dual build system (Bazel and CMake), and a comprehensive test suite driving itself.

3. Examine README for additional insights  
   - Confirms merging of GoogleTest and GoogleMock, C++17 requirement, CI approach, and documentation hosted on GitHub Pages.  
   - Highlights extension points (user‐defined assertions, event listeners) and integration with external tools (IDE plugins, TAP listeners).

4. Designing the system architecture diagram  
   a. Main components:  
      • Source modules: googletest core, googlemock core  
      • Build systems: Bazel pipeline, CMake pipeline  
      • CI environments: Linux, macOS, Windows presubmit runners  
      • Documentation generation: Jekyll engine → GitHub Pages  
      • External integrations: Abseil (future), IDE plugins, third-party runners  
      • Consumer layer: user projects linking against gtest/gmock libraries  
   b. Relationships and interactions:  
      • Arrows from source modules to both Bazel and CMake build boxes (compilation, packaging into static/shared libs)  
      • Build boxes feed test executables back into CI runners  
      • Docs folder → Jekyll → GitHub Pages (dashed arrow indicating “publish”)  
      • Consumer projects depend on built libraries (arrow from libs to user apps)  
      • External tools/plugins consume APIs or test binaries  
   c. Architectural patterns and design principles:  
      • Modular layering: libraries separated by functionality (testing vs. mocking)  
      • Dual‐build abstraction allowing consumers to choose Bazel or CMake  
      • Self-hosting test suite: the framework tests itself across platforms  
      • Extension points via listener interfaces and custom assertion macros  
   d. Relevant technologies:  
      • C++17  
      • Build: Bazel, CMake  
      • CI scripts: shell, batch  
      • Docs: Jekyll (Ruby), GitHub Pages  
      • Testing: Python‐based leak and output tests in addition to C++ tests

5. Guidelines for an open-source tool diagram  
   - Emphasize core functionality nodes (Test Runner, Mock Engine).  
   - Highlight extensibility points (Custom Assertions, Listeners, Parameterized tests).  
   - Show integration edges to external tools (IDEs, CI systems, TAP listeners).  
   - Illustrate where future dependencies (Abseil) will fit into the build graph.

6. Diagram elements to include  
   - Clear rectangular boxes for each component (e.g., “googlemock/src”, “googletest/include”)  
   - Directional arrows for data flow:  
       • Source → Build → Binaries → CI → Artifacts → Users  
       • Docs → Jekyll → GitHub Pages  
   - Color coding or shapes to distinguish:  
       • Source modules (blue)  
       • Build systems (green)  
       • CI environments (orange)  
       • Documentation (purple)  
       • Consumer/integration (gray)  

7. Level of detail  
   - Break down each library into its headers, sources, and tests if needed.  
   - Show both build engines in parallel to convey multi-build support.  
   - Include test runners (gtest_main, gmock_main) as subcomponents of build outputs.  
   - Capture CI presubmit scripts triggering cross-platform test runs.  

By following these guidelines, you’ll produce a comprehensive system design diagram that accurately captures GoogleTest’s modular architecture, build pipelines, CI processes, documentation flow, and integration points—providing clear, color-coded, and well-labeled visuals tailored to this open-source testing framework.  
</explanation>
